claim: 80 female C57BL/6JRj mice were purchased from Janvier at the age of 4 weeks.
source: 80 female C57BL/6JRj mice were purchased from Janvier at the age of 4 weeks and housed in standard polycarbonate cages (Type III, Tecniplast) in groups of five until the start of the experiment (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the experimental animals.

claim: At the age of 5 weeks, 40 mice were randomly selected and transferred into the enriched environment for three months.
source: At the age of 5 weeks, 40 mice were randomly selected and transferred into the enriched environment, where they stayed for three months (no restricted randomization).
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the experimental design.

claim: The enriched environment consisted of four quadratic polycarbonate cages (0.74 × 0.74 m) that were assembled in a row and connected by two plastic tubes each.
source: The enriched environment consisted of four quadratic polycarbonate cages (0.74 × 0.74 m) that were assembled in a row and connected by two plastic tubes each.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the enriched environment setup.

claim: The enriched environment covered an area of 2.19 m².
source: In total, the enriched environment covered an area of 2.19 m2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Control animals were housed in standard polycarbonate cages (36.5 × 20.7×14 cm) in groups of five.
source: Control animals were housed for the same period of time in standard polycarbonate cages (36.5 × 20.7×14 cm) connected to an individually ventilated cage system in groups of five.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing control housing conditions.

claim: Three weeks before sacrifice, mice were injected intraperitoneally with BrdU (50 mg/kg body weight) once per day for three consecutive days.
source: Three weeks before sacrifice, the mice were injected intraperitoneally with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU; 50 mg/kg body weight; dissolved in 0.9% NaCl). Injections were performed once per day for three consecutive days.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing BrdU injection protocol.

claim: At the beginning of the experiment, no differences in weight existed between the two groups.
source: At the beginning of the experiment, no differences in weight existed between the two groups, confirming initial similarity between the randomized experimental mice.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section supported by longitudinal weight measurements.

claim: Five weeks after the start of the experiment, ENR mice were significantly lighter than mice housed in control cages (CTRL).
source: However, five weeks after the start of the experiment, ENR mice were significantly lighter than mice housed in control cages (CTRL).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section supported by longitudinal weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference in body weight between ENR and CTRL mice remained constant throughout the experiment.
source: The difference in body weight remained constant throughout the experiment and indicated, together with the significantly shorter body length in ENR mice (Figure 2B), that housing of mice in ENR reduces body size.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section supported by longitudinal weight measurements.

claim: ENR mice had significantly shorter body length than CTRL mice.
source: The difference in body weight remained constant throughout the experiment and indicated, together with the significantly shorter body length in ENR mice (Figure 2B), that housing of mice in ENR reduces body size.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 2B showing body length measurements.

claim: Housing of mice in ENR reduces body size.
source: The difference in body weight remained constant throughout the experiment and indicated, together with the significantly shorter body length in ENR mice (Figure 2B), that housing of mice in ENR reduces body size.
evidence: Direct conclusion in the results section based on body weight and length measurements.

claim: No differences in brain weights were detected between ENR and CTRL mice.
source: By contrast, no differences in brain weights were detected between ENR and CTRL mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The groups did not differ in the variances of body length, body weight and brain weight at any measured time point.
source: The groups did not differ in the variances of body length, body weight and brain weight at any measured time point, suggesting that long-term ENR does not stimulate the development of inter-individual differences in gross body morphology.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on variance analysis.

claim: Long-term ENR does not stimulate the development of inter-individual differences in gross body morphology.
source: The groups did not differ in the variances of body length, body weight and brain weight at any measured time point, suggesting that long-term ENR does not stimulate the development of inter-individual differences in gross body morphology.
evidence: Direct conclusion in the results section based on variance analysis of body morphology measurements.

claim: ENR mice traveled longer distances during the first OF trial.
source: ENR mice traveled longer distances during the first OF trial, but showed less locomotion in the second OF trial (Figure 3C) and throughout the NOR test (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: ENR mice showed less locomotion in the second OF trial.
source: ENR mice traveled longer distances during the first OF trial, but showed less locomotion in the second OF trial (Figure 3C) and throughout the NOR test (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: ENR mice showed less locomotion throughout the NOR test.
source: ENR mice traveled longer distances during the first OF trial, but showed less locomotion in the second OF trial (Figure 3C) and throughout the NOR test (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: No significant differences were found in the variance of locomotion in any of the OF or NOR trials.
source: No significant differences were found in the variance of locomotion in any of the OF or NOR trials.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on variance analysis of locomotion data.

claim: On both days, ENR mice had significantly lower RE than CTRL animals.
source: On both days, ENR mice had significantly lower RE than CTRL animals.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on roaming entropy measurements.

claim: On day 2, ENR mice showed a significantly greater variance in RE.
source: Moreover, on day 2, ENR mice showed a significantly greater variance in RE, suggesting a higher range of habituation to the OF among ENR mice.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on variance analysis of roaming entropy.

claim: ENR mice showed a higher range of habituation to the OF.
source: Moreover, on day 2, ENR mice showed a significantly greater variance in RE, suggesting a higher range of habituation to the OF among ENR mice.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the results section based on variance in roaming entropy.

claim: Both ENR and CTRL animals habituated to the OF arena, as indicated by a decrease in RE between the trials.
source: Indeed, both ENR and CTRL animals habituated to the OF arena, as indicated by a decrease in RE between the trials (Figure 3G).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 3G showing habituation data.

claim: Habituation was more pronounced and exhibited higher variance in ENR mice.
source: However, habituation was more pronounced and exhibited higher variance in ENR mice.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on habituation measurements.

claim: In the NOR test, ENR mice showed a significantly higher variance in the duration of their exploration of the objects when compared to CTRL mice.
source: In the NOR test, ENR mice showed a significantly higher variance in the duration of their exploration of the objects when compared to CTRL mice (Figure 3H), indicating that ENR increases the inter-individual variability in exploratory behavior.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 3H.

claim: ENR increases the inter-individual variability in exploratory behavior.
source: In the NOR test, ENR mice showed a significantly higher variance in the duration of their exploration of the objects when compared to CTRL mice (Figure 3H), indicating that ENR increases the inter-individual variability in exploratory behavior.
evidence: Direct conclusion in the results section based on variance in object exploration.

claim: Some individuals among ENR mice explored objects for much longer than any of the control animals.
source: Although some individuals among ENR mice explored objects for much longer than any of the control animals, the median of the entire ENR group was not shifted compared to that of the CTRL group.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on object exploration data.

claim: The median of the entire ENR group was not shifted compared to that of the CTRL group in object exploration.
source: Although some individuals among ENR mice explored objects for much longer than any of the control animals, the median of the entire ENR group was not shifted compared to that of the CTRL group.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on object exploration data.

claim: A trend towards a preference for the new object was found only in the ENR mice and not in the CTRL group.
source: Finally, to examine the effect of ENR on the recognition memory of individual mice, we analyzed the ability to discriminate a new object from an old one in the NOR test. A trend towards a preference for the new object was found only in the ENR mice and not in the CTRL group (Figure 3I).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 3I showing discrimination index.

claim: The performance of ENR mice on the rotarod was superior to that of CTRL mice in all trials.
source: The performance of ENR mice on the rotarod was superior to that of CTRL mice in all trials (Figure 3J), indicating that ENR stimulates motor coordination and, presumably, fitness.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 3J.

claim: ENR stimulates motor coordination and, presumably, fitness.
source: The performance of ENR mice on the rotarod was superior to that of CTRL mice in all trials (Figure 3J), indicating that ENR stimulates motor coordination and, presumably, fitness.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the results section based on rotarod performance.

claim: Initially, ENR mice showed a greater variance in their rotarod performance compared to that of CTRL.
source: Initially, ENR mice also showed a greater variance in their performance compared to that of CTRL, but while both groups improved in the task, this difference gradually disappeared.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on variance analysis of rotarod performance.

claim: While both groups improved in the rotarod task, the variance difference gradually disappeared.
source: Initially, ENR mice also showed a greater variance in their performance compared to that of CTRL, but while both groups improved in the task, this difference gradually disappeared.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on longitudinal rotarod performance data.

claim: ENR promotes the development of inter-individual differences in specific interactions with the environment, but not in pure locomotor activity.
source: Together, we conclude that ENR promotes the development of inter-individual differences in specific interactions with the environment, but not in pure locomotor activity.
evidence: Direct conclusion in the results section based on behavioral data.

claim: No differences in the means or variances of the numbers of proliferating cells in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus were observed between ENR and CTRL mice.
source: No differences in the means or variances of the numbers of proliferating cells in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus were observed between ENR and CTRL mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 4F showing Ki67 quantification.

claim: A significant increase in the means and variances of the numbers of BrdU-positive cells was found in animals housed in ENR.
source: By contrast, we found a significant increase in the means and variances of the numbers of BrdU-positive cells in animals housed in ENR (Figure 4G), highlighting the specific effect of ENR on the survival of new-born cells.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 4G.

claim: ENR has a specific effect on the survival of new-born cells.
source: By contrast, we found a significant increase in the means and variances of the numbers of BrdU-positive cells in animals housed in ENR (Figure 4G), highlighting the specific effect of ENR on the survival of new-born cells.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the results section based on BrdU quantification.

claim: The variances in the survival of both neurons and astrocytes were higher in the ENR group than in the CTRL animals.
source: Co-localization of BrdU-positive cells with the neuronal marker NeuN and the astrocytic marker S100β (Figure 4E) showed that the variances in the survival of both neurons and astrocytes were higher in the ENR group than in the CTRL animals (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figures 4E, 4H, and 4I.

claim: An increase in the total number of cells was only found in the neuronal cell population.
source: An increase in the total number of cells was, however, only found in the neuronal cell population.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on cell type-specific quantification.

claim: ENR increases inter-individual variability in the survival of new-born neurons and astrocytes but not in the proliferation of precursor cells in the dentate gyrus.
source: These results indicate that ENR increases inter-individual variability in the survival of new-born neurons and astrocytes but not in the proliferation of precursor cells in the dentate gyrus.
evidence: Direct conclusion in the results section based on neurogenesis measurements.

claim: The volume of the entire hippocampus did not differ between ENR and CTRL mice.
source: The volume of the entire hippocampus did not differ between ENR and CTRL mice (Figure 5H), but the volume of the dentate gyrus was significantly increased in ENR mice (Figure 5I).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 5H.

claim: The volume of the dentate gyrus was significantly increased in ENR mice.
source: The volume of the entire hippocampus did not differ between ENR and CTRL mice (Figure 5H), but the volume of the dentate gyrus was significantly increased in ENR mice (Figure 5I).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 5I.

claim: IMF and the hilus, but not SMF, were significantly larger in ENR animals than in CTRL mice.
source: Furthermore, IMF (Figure 5J) and the hilus (Figure 5L), but not SMF (Figure 5K), were significantly larger in ENR animals than in CTRL mice.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with references to Figures 5J, 5K, and 5L.

claim: None of the hippocampal parameters showed different variances depending on housing conditions.
source: None of these parameters showed different variances depending on housing conditions.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on variance analysis of hippocampal volumes.

claim: ENR differentially influenced various aspects of hippocampal plasticity.
source: This suggests that ENR differentially influenced various aspects of hippocampal plasticity, while showing that the increased inter-individual variability that was triggered by ENR was specific to adult neurogenesis.
evidence: Direct conclusion in the results section based on hippocampal morphometry data.

claim: The increased inter-individual variability that was triggered by ENR was specific to adult neurogenesis.
source: This suggests that ENR differentially influenced various aspects of hippocampal plasticity, while showing that the increased inter-individual variability that was triggered by ENR was specific to adult neurogenesis.
evidence: Direct conclusion in the results section based on comparison of variance effects across different brain structures.

claim: No differences were detected in the thickness of the entorhinal, cingulate, or motor cortex between CTRL and ENR mice.
source: Although we did not detect differences in the thickness of any of these cortices between CTRL and ENR mice (Figure 5M–O), the motor cortex thickness showed a significantly higher variance in the ENR group (Figure 5O).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with references to Figures 5M, 5N, and 5O.

claim: The motor cortex thickness showed a significantly higher variance in the ENR group.
source: Although we did not detect differences in the thickness of any of these cortices between CTRL and ENR mice (Figure 5M–O), the motor cortex thickness showed a significantly higher variance in the ENR group (Figure 5O).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 5O.

claim: ENR animals had smaller adrenal glands and livers.
source: In agreement with lower body weights, ENR animals had smaller adrenal glands and livers (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with references to Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The levels of plasma corticosterone did not differ between the groups.
source: The levels of plasma corticosterone, which is synthesized in the adrenal gland and is used as an indicator of animal stress, did not differ between the groups (Figure 6C).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: ENR mice had significantly lower plasma cholesterol levels.
source: Moreover, significantly lower plasma cholesterol levels (Figure 6D) in ENR mice but no differences in triglyceride and glucose levels were seen when comparing ENR and CTRL mice (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: No differences in triglyceride and glucose levels were seen when comparing ENR and CTRL mice.
source: Moreover, significantly lower plasma cholesterol levels (Figure 6D) in ENR mice but no differences in triglyceride and glucose levels were seen when comparing ENR and CTRL mice (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with references to Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: No variance differences between the two groups were detected in any of the measured metabolic parameters.
source: No variance differences between the two groups were detected in any of the measured metabolic parameters.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on variance analysis of metabolic measurements.

claim: Strong correlation between two traits would point towards shared regulatory mechanisms in the control of such parameters.
source: Strong correlation between two traits would point towards shared regulatory mechanisms in the control of such parameters.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section explaining the interpretation of correlations.

claim: Few significant correlations were observed in either housing condition, suggesting that the majority of the traits were independent of each other.
source: We observed few significant correlations in either housing condition, which suggests that the majority of the traits were independent of each other.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: In both animal groups, significant positive correlations of roaming entropy and object exploration between trials of the OF and NOR tests were found, respectively.
source: In both animal groups, we found significant positive correlations of roaming entropy and object exploration between trials of the OF and NOR tests, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: The correlations between trials indicate that the recorded behaviors were reliable and characteristic for each individual.
source: These correlations indicate that the recorded behaviors were reliable and characteristic for each individual.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: ENR weakened correlations between trials in NOR, as well as the negative association of object exploration to OF habituation.
source: ENR, however, weakened correlations between trials in NOR, as well as the negative association of object exploration to OF habituation, hinting towards more specific responses of animals to the environment (e.g. exposure to novel objects or their placement).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: Housing in ENR led to remodeling of the associations between the brain structures and behavior.
source: Housing in ENR led to remodeling of the associations between the brain structures and behavior (Figure 7A).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: ENR uncoupled the negative correlations of object exploration in NOR test and of rotarod performance to the volume of the hippocampus.
source: ENR uncoupled the negative correlations of object exploration in NOR test and of rotarod performance to the volume of the hippocampus.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: Habituation to the OF arena was negatively associated with the size of the IMF and positively correlated with the motor cortex thickness in CTRL mice, but not ENR mice.
source: Similarly, habituation to the OF arena was negatively associated with the size of the IMF and positively correlated with the motor cortex thickness in CTRL mice, but not ENR mice.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: Hippocampal neurogenesis did not show significant correlation with any of the assayed phenotypes.
source: Hippocampal neurogenesis did not show significant correlation with any of the assayed phenotypes.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: Metabolic phenotypes, namely plasma glucose, cholesterol and triglycerides were positively correlated in both housing conditions.
source: Metabolic phenotypes, namely plasma glucose, cholesterol and triglycerides were positively correlated in both housing conditions, but these relationships were weakened by ENR (Figure 7B).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: The relationships between metabolic phenotypes were weakened by ENR.
source: Metabolic phenotypes, namely plasma glucose, cholesterol and triglycerides were positively correlated in both housing conditions, but these relationships were weakened by ENR (Figure 7B).
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: Plasma triglycerides correlated positively to the liver size in both groups.
source: As expected, plasma triglycerides correlated positively to the liver size in both groups.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: ENR changed the sign of the correlations between object exploration in NOR test and plasma cholesterol from positive to negative.
source: ENR changed the sign of the correlations between object exploration in NOR test and plasma cholesterol from positive to negative.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: ENR promoted negative correlation between plasma glucose and rotarod performance.
source: It also promoted negative correlation between plasma glucose and rotarod performance, suggesting that the fitness acquired by ENR mice has a metabolic component.
evidence: Direct statement in the results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: The fitness acquired by ENR mice has a metabolic component.
source: It also promoted negative correlation between plasma glucose and rotarod performance, suggesting that the fitness acquired by ENR mice has a metabolic component.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the results section based on correlation between glucose and rotarod performance.

claim: ENR is a suitable model to dissect processes leading to brain individualization.
source: Here we established that ENR is a suitable model to dissect processes leading to brain individualization.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section summarizing the main conclusion.

claim: Different traits are not uniformly affected by the stimuli.
source: We have shown that different traits are not uniformly affected by the stimuli and, besides effects on the mean, effects on variance could also be observed for certain parameters.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: The effects in which ENR increases differences between individuals in the group cluster in variables related to behavior and adult neurogenesis.
source: The effects in which ENR increases differences between individuals in the group cluster in variables related to behavior and adult neurogenesis.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section summarizing the pattern of variance effects.

claim: With 40 individuals in each experimental group, a 5% pre-set significance level in a two-tailed variance test enabled detection of an effect size of 2.5 (ratio of variances) with power of 0.8.
source: With 40 individuals in each experimental group, a 5% pre-set significance level in a two-tailed variance test enabled us to detect an effect size of 2.5 (ratio of variances) with power of 0.8.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section explaining the statistical power of the study.

claim: Significant p-values in the experiment were not uniformly distributed across all phenotypes.
source: Significant p-values in our experiment were not uniformly distributed across all phenotypes, supporting our view that we achieved a balance between false-negative and false-positive error rates sufficient to provide a coherent overview of the effects of ENR on a wide variety of traits.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section supporting the validity of the statistical approach.

claim: ENR elicits profound effects on brain plasticity and behavior.
source: It has long been known that ENR elicits profound effects on brain plasticity and behavior (Mohammed et al., 2002; Sale et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement in the discussion section supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ENR mice habituate faster to an open field, which has been interpreted as improved spatial processing.
source: We have previously found, for example, that ENR mice habituate faster to an open field, and this observation has been interpreted as improved spatial processing (Kempermann and Gage, 1999).
evidence: Statement in the discussion section supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Short 2 min trials in the NOR task precluded efficient familiarization with objects.
source: Short 2 min trials in our NOR task precluded efficient familiarization with objects (Melani et al., 2017), which explains the lack of preference towards the new object.
evidence: Statement in the discussion section with citation explaining the behavioral result.

claim: The current study highlights that ENR also induced substantial inter-individual variability in specific behavioral parameters.
source: The current study now highlights that ENR also induced substantial inter-individual variability in specific behavioral parameters.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section summarizing a key finding.

claim: Active participation with the outer world and habitat that manifests itself in the individual range of locomotion within that world (roaming entropy) is a major driving force of brain plasticity.
source: We have previously argued that the active participation with the outer world and habitat that manifests itself in the individual range of locomotion within that world (roaming entropy) is a major driving force of brain plasticity, presumably not limited to adult hippocampal neurogenesis (Freund et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement in the discussion section presenting a hypothesis supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Large cage area and toys to interact with provide considerable motor stimulation even if running wheels are not supplied.
source: The improvement of rotarod performance in the ENR mice observed in this study implies that, even if the running wheels are not supplied, large cage area and toys to interact with provide considerable motor stimulation (Kempermann and Gage, 1999), which, together with elevated variance of the motor cortex thickness, suggest that ENR strongly affects the plasticity of motor responses.
evidence: Statement in the discussion section with citation, interpreting the rotarod results.

claim: ENR strongly affects the plasticity of motor responses.
source: The improvement of rotarod performance in the ENR mice observed in this study implies that, even if the running wheels are not supplied, large cage area and toys to interact with provide considerable motor stimulation (Kempermann and Gage, 1999), which, together with elevated variance of the motor cortex thickness, suggest that ENR strongly affects the plasticity of motor responses.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the discussion section based on rotarod and motor cortex data.

claim: Activation of motor cortex by ENR has widespread modulatory effects on other cortical areas.
source: It has been proposed that activation of motor cortex by ENR has widespread modulatory effects on other cortical areas (Sale et al., 2014; Di Garbo et al., 2011; Niell and Stryker, 2010).
evidence: Statement in the discussion section supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The large size of both the control and the ENR groups in the present study allowed corroboration of the finding that long-term ENR induces variability in the survival of new-born neurons (F-test: p=0.00004).
source: Our previous report suggested that long-term ENR induces variability in the survival of new-born neurons (Freund et al., 2013). The large size of both the control and the ENR groups in the present study allowed us to corroborate that finding (F-test: p=0.00004).
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section with statistical evidence and citation to previous work.

claim: Over prolonged periods of time, enrichment might have subtle pro-proliferative effects.
source: Although the effect of ENR on the mean numbers of proliferating cells did not reach the significance threshold applied here (p=0.09), together with our previous report (Kempermann et al., 2002), this study suggests that over prolonged periods of time, enrichment might have subtle pro-proliferative effects.
evidence: Statement in the discussion section with citation, interpreting non-significant trend.

claim: The behavioral significance of proliferating cells as such has not yet been shown.
source: Proliferating cells are a substrate on which selection mechanisms can act, but their behavioral significance as such has not yet been shown.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section about the current state of knowledge.

claim: ENR does not trigger individuality in precursor cell proliferation, indicating that individualization mechanisms act selectively only on those aspects of neurogenesis that are relevant for interactions with the environment.
source: The fact that ENR does not trigger individuality in precursor cell proliferation indicates that individualization mechanisms act selectively only on those aspects of neurogenesis that are relevant for interactions with the environment.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the discussion section based on the pattern of variance effects.

claim: In the study by Freund et al., 2013, 21% of the variance in adult neurogenesis could be explained by differences in cumulative roaming entropy.
source: In contrast to the study by Freund et al., 2013, in which 21% of the variance in adult neurogenesis could be explained by differences in cumulative roaming entropy (RE), an aggregated measure of the longitudinal behavioral trajectory, the current analysis detected no correlation between the number of newborn neurons and any of the cross-sectionally measured behaviors, including RE measured in the OF test.
evidence: Statement in the discussion section citing a specific finding from previous work.

claim: The current analysis detected no correlation between the number of newborn neurons and any of the cross-sectionally measured behaviors, including RE measured in the OF test.
source: In contrast to the study by Freund et al., 2013, in which 21% of the variance in adult neurogenesis could be explained by differences in cumulative roaming entropy (RE), an aggregated measure of the longitudinal behavioral trajectory, the current analysis detected no correlation between the number of newborn neurons and any of the cross-sectionally measured behaviors, including RE measured in the OF test.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section based on correlation analysis.

claim: The behavior in the familiar environment of the ENR cage is presumably driven by other factors and can be influenced by the group interactions.
source: The behavior in the familiar environment of the ENR cage, however, is presumably driven by other factors and can be influenced by the group interactions (Shemesh et al., 2013), whereas the OF test reflects an individual response of an animal to novel situations and might, therefore, constitute a different construct.
evidence: Statement in the discussion section with citation, explaining differences in behavioral contexts.

claim: The OF test reflects an individual response of an animal to novel situations and might constitute a different construct from behavior in the ENR cage.
source: The behavior in the familiar environment of the ENR cage, however, is presumably driven by other factors and can be influenced by the group interactions (Shemesh et al., 2013), whereas the OF test reflects an individual response of an animal to novel situations and might, therefore, constitute a different construct.
evidence: Statement in the discussion section explaining the interpretation of behavioral measures.

claim: The mossy fiber projection, and especially its infra-pyramidal blade (IMF), is highly plastic in mice.
source: The mossy fiber projection, and especially its infra-pyramidal blade (IMF), is highly plastic in mice (Crusio et al., 1989; Schwegler et al., 1981) and ENR can modulate its size (Römer et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement in the discussion section supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ENR can modulate the size of the mossy fiber projection.
source: The mossy fiber projection, and especially its infra-pyramidal blade (IMF), is highly plastic in mice (Crusio et al., 1989; Schwegler et al., 1981) and ENR can modulate its size (Römer et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement in the discussion section supported by citation.

claim: An increased volume of the IMF but no effect on the variance of this volume was found after 3 months of ENR.
source: We found an increased volume of the IMF but no effect on the variance of this volume after 3 months of ENR, suggesting that even for aspects of hippocampal plasticity there is no simple parallelism in the effects of ENR.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section based on IMF volumetry data.

claim: Even for aspects of hippocampal plasticity there is no simple parallelism in the effects of ENR.
source: We found an increased volume of the IMF but no effect on the variance of this volume after 3 months of ENR, suggesting that even for aspects of hippocampal plasticity there is no simple parallelism in the effects of ENR.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the discussion section based on differential effects on hippocampal structures.

claim: Adult-generated neurons contribute to the IMF.
source: Adult-generated neurons contribute to the IMF (Römer et al., 2011), yet we did not observe a correlation between numbers of new neurons and IMF volume within either housing group, impliying that, under physiological conditions, mechanisms other than adult neurogenesis determine the bulk of the IMF.
evidence: Statement in the discussion section supported by citation.

claim: No correlation was observed between numbers of new neurons and IMF volume within either housing group.
source: Adult-generated neurons contribute to the IMF (Römer et al., 2011), yet we did not observe a correlation between numbers of new neurons and IMF volume within either housing group, impliying that, under physiological conditions, mechanisms other than adult neurogenesis determine the bulk of the IMF.
evidence: Direct statement in the discussion section based on correlation analysis.

claim: Under physiological conditions, mechanisms other than adult neurogenesis determine the bulk of the IMF.
source: Adult-generated neurons contribute to the IMF (Römer et al., 2011), yet we did not observe a correlation between numbers of new neurons and IMF volume within either housing group, impliying that, under physiological conditions, mechanisms other than adult neurogenesis determine the bulk of the IMF.
evidence: Direct interpretation in the discussion section based on lack of correlation.

claim: This finding is in agreement with the results from the screen in the mouse genetic reference population.
source: This finding is in agreement with the results from the screen in the mouse genetic reference population (Krebs et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement in the discussion section supported by citation.

claim: Cortex thickness changes upon enrichment of the environment have been reported in the older literature and were the cornerstone of the growing impact of the ENR paradigm in the 1970s.
source: Cortex thickness changes upon enrichment of the environment have been reported in the older literature and were the cornerstone of the growing impact of the ENR paradigm in the 1970s (reviewed in Diamond, 2001; Rosenzweig and Bennett, 1996).
